content: Vaginal candidiasis, also known as thrush or moniliasis, is a common and often distressing infection for many women, with an increased prevalence during pregnancy. Importantly, there is no evidence to suggest that vaginal candidiasis during pregnancy poses any harm to the baby. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of various treatments for vaginal candidiasis in pregnant women. The analysis included randomized trials that investigated different treatment methods for this condition during pregnancy. The review incorporated data from ten trials. Based on five of these trials, imidazole-based antifungal medications were found to be significantly more effective than nystatin in treating vaginal candidiasis during pregnancy. The odds ratio for this comparison was 0.21, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 0.16 to 0.29. In one trial, nystatin was shown to be as effective as hydrargaphen, with an odds ratio of 0.29 and a 95% confidence interval of 0.05 to 1.84. Additionally, a trial comparing clotrimazole to a placebo demonstrated that clotrimazole was significantly more effective, with an odds ratio of 0.14 and a 95% confidence interval of 0.06 to 0.31. Regarding the duration of treatment, single-dose therapy was found to be neither more nor less effective than treatment courses lasting three or four days. However, two trials involving 81 women revealed that a four-day treatment regimen was less effective than a seven-day regimen, with an odds ratio of 11.7 and a 95% confidence interval of 4.21 to 29.15. Furthermore, based on two trials, a seven-day treatment course was found to be equally effective as a 14-day course, with an odds ratio of 0.41 and a 95% confidence interval of 0.16 to 1.05. In terms of comparing different antifungal agents, terconazole was found to be as effective as clotrimazole, with an odds ratio of 1.41 and a 95% confidence interval of 0.28 to 7.10. The authors concluded that topical imidazole antifungal agents appear to be more effective than nystatin for the treatment of symptomatic vaginal candidiasis during pregnancy. Additionally, a seven-day treatment course may be necessary for pregnant women, as shorter courses commonly used in non-pregnant women may not be as effective. However, it is important to note that seven citations awaiting classification at the time of this review may potentially alter these conclusions once they are assessed.
